S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage to the regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, and provide a complete incident report within 5 business days. They must promptly notify affected customers of an incident that may present a safety risk, and no later than 24 hours after notifying the regulator.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or property damage to the regulator within 24 hours of learning of it, and provide a complete incident report within 5 business days. They must promptly notify affected customers of an incident that may present a safety risk, and no later than 24 hours after notifying the regulator. Reports must include the model, unit identification where available, incident circumstances, known injuries or damage, and actions taken. Manufacturers must also submit an annual accounting of thermal incidents, including incidents not previously reported, and explain any reporting gaps.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% for every model.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol. The maximum permitted failure rate is 5% for every model. Manufacturers must submit per-model results and supporting records to the regulator and provide results directly to customers who buy or are considering that model; individual-company per-model failure rates need not be published to the general public. For models already on the market when this standard takes effect, manufacturers have six months to complete initial testing and submit results, and must provide a testing schedule to the regulator. A model found above the limit must be reported promptly to the regulator and affected customers, and the manufacturer must submit corrective-action milestones and retest at least every six months. Manufacturers have 36 months from the standard’s effective date to bring existing models into compliance before they may no longer be newly placed on the market. Regulators may require earlier sales suspension or other measures where incident evidence indicates an imminent serious risk. Manufacturers must implement regulator-approved corrective actions for units already installed.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New home battery models placed on the market beginning two years after this standard takes effect must support remote emergency shut-off. S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New home battery models placed on the market beginning two years after this standard takes effect must support remote emergency shut-off. Manufacturers must provide clear instructions for its use and safeguards against unauthorized activation. For units already installed when the standard takes effect, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or replacement pathway and complete required upgrades within six years, prioritizing units presenting the greatest documented risk.

parameters.quote: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect. Manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence that the suppression system is effective and does not introduce additional material safety risks.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect. Manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence that the suppression system is effective and does not introduce additional material safety risks.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New home battery units must include built-in fire suppression beginning 36 months after this standard takes effect. Manufacturers must provide regulators with evidence that the suppression system is effective and does not introduce additional material safety risks.

parameters.quote: A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year; the manufacturer must promptly notify regulators and affected customers, stop distribution, and implement the regulator-approved recall. Regulators may require a recall below that threshold when evidence indicates an imminent serious risk.

S5_customer_disclosure.rule_summary: A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year; the manufacturer must promptly notify regulators and affected customers, stop distribution, and implement the regulator-approved recall. Regulators may require a recall below that threshold when evidence indicates an imminent serious risk.
S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Before purchase, customers must receive clear information on material battery hazards, safe installation and operation, emergency response, and how to report an incident. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of safety risks and provide updates on corrective actions. For each model, the annual thermal-incident rate must be calculated as qualifying thermal incidents involving that model during the calendar year divided by that model’s installed units at year-end, multiplied by 100,000. Count incidents when they occur, including incidents reported late; include late-reported incidents in the next submission and correct prior calculations when needed. Manufacturers must keep auditable incident and installed-unit records and submit annual calculations and any corrections to regulators for verification. They must also make each model’s verified annual rate available to current and prospective customers. A recall is mandatory when any model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year; the manufacturer must promptly notify regulators and affected customers, stop distribution, and implement the regulator-approved recall. Regulators may require a recall below that threshold when evidence indicates an imminent serious risk.

judge_section_notes: S1 is strict: all incidents reported within 24 hours, customer notice within 24 hours, no phase-in. S2 keeps a 5% limit but gives existing models a 36-month transition with no interim cap, and results go to customers/regulators but not the public, which favors Northwind. S5 mandates recall at 8/100k with no transition, severely hurting Halcyon given Ember 8's 9.9 rate; S4's 36-month suppression deadline meets Halcyon's red line, but overall the deal favors Northwind.
